text: TET-93 / TET-56: a bounded reply

This memo decides what a bounded tetel reply is, and applies that decision to the three replies TET-93 names: `look`, `fact` and `query`. It is the shared decision that queue items A2 to A7 wait on. `run` (A5) and `check` (A6) are held under the same bound here only by a backstop; shaping them properly is their own work, as is what the exclusion note should contain (A4) and how much a capture may store (A12). All of these are deferred explicitly, in the last section. Everything below was read against one pinned worktree.
The defect, and the threshold behind it

The stub is Claude Code's, not tetel's. Past a size threshold it writes an MCP reply to a file and hands the model the path instead. A grounder or attacker restricted to tetel's own tools has no way to open that path, so the reply is simply gone, and nothing in the stub says what was in it. Both tickets had to infer the threshold from spills. It no longer needs inferring: the installed binary sets it at 50,000 characters for an unannotated MCP tool, and lets a server set its own per tool through an annotation. That changes the premise TET-56's f3 memo was built on, which held that tetel cannot learn the caller's cap and so has to guess below it. Tetel still cannot read the cap at run time, but for the client this loop runs in, it can declare one.

Today tetel measures none of its replies, so every verb that reads the tree or lists the workspace can cross the threshold. TET-93's `fact` case needs correcting on one point. `fact` does not echo captured output, as the ticket's proposal assumed. Its size comes from `folded`, which repeats each pending entry's label in full, and a search's label ends in the exclusion note that lists every git-ignored path. So the 130k-character `fact` reply was TET-92's defect surfacing through `fact`. It was not an output echo.
The budget, and the threshold tetel declares

A bounded reply is one whose content text is at most `REPLY_BUDGET`, 32768 UTF-8 bytes. Bytes are the unit because they are what tetel can count cheaply, and they are safe: JavaScript's string length never exceeds UTF-8 byte length, so a reply within 32768 bytes is within 32768 of Claude Code's characters as well. 32768 is under the 50,000 characters an unannotated tool gets, so the budget alone keeps tetel clear of the spill for a client that ignores what tetel declares.

Tetel also declares its own threshold, `_meta["anthropic/maxResultSizeChars"] = 100000` on every tool it lists, which rmcp can already emit. The declaration is headroom and not permission to send more. The budget stays at 32768, and 100000 covers the case this design could not rule out: that Claude Code counts `content` and `structured_content` together, and `structured()` puts the same JSON in both. The 500000 ceiling was not taken, because a reply that is never spilled still costs the caller its context. One residual risk remains open: a per-tool-name override inside Claude Code, whose source was not traced, would win over the declaration. The budget is what protects against that.
One enforcer: the backstop in `call_tool`

"Every reply is bounded" cannot rest on each verb remembering to bound itself. The next verb, or the next field added to an existing one, would break it silently. `call_tool` is written by hand so that every tool call goes through one place, and that makes it the enforcer. After the router returns, it measures a completed result. An over-budget result becomes text only: a prefix cut at a line boundary, then a marker giving the bytes shown against the total and saying that the capture is intact. `structured_content` is dropped, because a truncated JSON document is no longer JSON. Errors are small, fixed strings and pass through unshaped. The backstop is a floor, and it is not how a verb is supposed to answer: `look`, `fact` and `query` shape their own replies below, and a reply the backstop has to cut counts as a defect in the verb that produced it. Until A5 and A6 land, `run` and `check` are held under the bound by the backstop alone.
Shaping the three verbs TET-93 names

**`look` on a file.** A whole-file `look` pages instead of spilling. The reply carries whole lines from the start of the selection up to the budget, and it ends by naming the next range to ask for. The capture is narrowed to match: the pending entry holds only the lines returned, and its label names that range, so a fact minted from it never claims the author saw more than was shown. That keeps the property every other extent has, that what was looked at equals what was seen. Refusal was rejected because it gives the author nothing to work with. An outline (signatures and headings) was rejected because it needs a parser for every language tetel might open, and because an outline is a summary, not the text a fact is minted from.

**`look` with `grep`.** A search cannot page the way a file does, because a census has to capture every match, so this follows TET-56 f3 as written. The capture keeps grep's whole stdout, and the reply carries whole match lines up to the budget, with the shortfall stated in both the reply and the label. The exclusion note counts against the budget too. When it does not fit, it falls back to counts, and what it should list at all is left to A4. Paging a grep is deferred; for now the marker points to a narrower root or pattern.

**`fact`.** The parts the author has to act on are always kept: the id, the action, the attention kinds with their guidance, and `verify`. The three lists that can grow without limit (`folded`, the refusals since the previous fact, and attention's extent labels) are bounded twice. Each entry is cut to `ENTRY_CAP` (1024 bytes), then whole entries are kept until the budget, and whatever is left over becomes a count with a pointer to `query facts`. Minting is not affected; only what the reply reports is shortened.

**`query`.** Listings page by id: `from` names the first record, whole records follow in id order up to the budget, and a trailer names the next `from`. Labels in a listing are cut to `ENTRY_CAP`. Anyone who needs a record in full asks for it by `id`, and gets it uncut. The CLI gets the same flags, so the two surfaces do not diverge.

"Every reply is bounded" cannot rest on each verb remembering to bound itself. The next verb, or the next field added to an existing one, would break it silently. `call_tool` is written by hand so that every tool call goes through one place, and that makes it the enforcer. After the router returns, it measures every outcome. An over-budget completed result, error or not, becomes text only: a prefix cut at a line boundary, then a marker giving the bytes shown against the total and saying that the capture is intact. `structured_content` is dropped, because a truncated JSON document is no longer JSON. A protocol error's message is cut the same way, so no outcome is exempt. The backstop is a floor, and it is not how a verb is supposed to answer: `look`, `fact` and `query` shape their own replies below, and a reply the backstop has to cut counts as a defect in the verb that produced it. Until A5 and A6 land, `run` and `check` are held under the bound by the backstop alone.
why: Follow C8: errors are measured too, not exempt.

text: Deferred, and how the slices are proven

Each of these stays with its own queue item: shaping `run` (A5) and `check` (A6), what the exclusion note should contain (A4), how much a capture may store (A12), `query prose --ids` (TET-66), and paging a grep. Until they land, the backstop is what bounds their replies. This memo fixes the two things every one of them has to fit under, the budget and the marker, and leaves each item free to decide how its own reply is shaped.

Each slice ships with its tests, and each test has to be shown red against a revert of the change it guards. The annotation test compares two exact sets, the tools listed against the tools annotated, so that a new tool without the annotation fails it. The backstop test includes an under-budget contrast, to show that shaping never touches a reply it does not need to. The grep test checks the reply and the capture separately, because the defect it guards against is a reply that fits the budget while the capture has quietly lost matches. The last test says the backstop never fires for a verb this memo shapes, which is how "a cut reply is a defect" gets enforced.
One enforcer: the backstop in `call_tool`

text: **`fact`.** The attacker found a second route for TET-93's reply to overflow. What is always kept is small and fixed in size: the id, the action, `verify`'s status, and how many attention entries there are. Everything that can grow is bounded twice: `folded`, the refusals since the previous fact, the attention entries and their labels, and the evidence quoted in `verify`'s findings. Minting is not affected; only what the reply reports is shortened.

text: **`fact`.** Two routes let TET-93's reply overflow, and there is one trap in closing them. The first route: each attention entry's guidance repeated every extent label of the fact, uncut, once per path the note names outside its extent. That is fixed in `scope::advice` itself, which now lists at most four labels, each cut, and a count, so the CLI and MCP keep sharing one text. The second route is `folded`, which is bounded like the other lists: each entry is cut to `ENTRY_CAP` (1024 bytes), then whole entries are kept until the budget, and whatever is left over becomes a count with a pointer to `query facts`. The trap is `verify`. A finding is marked delivered while the reply is being built, so a finding that shaping drops is never offered again. So shaping follows a fixed priority. `verify` comes first and is never dropped, with each finding's quoted text cut to 512 bytes. Then attention, then `folded`, then refusals. A verification too large to fit even then is left undelivered and offered again, which matches `verify_block`'s own rule: a finding may be shown twice, but never lost. Its withheld tail stays readable only through the CLI's `verify-report` until a partial delivery cursor exists. Minting is not affected; only what the reply reports is shortened.
why: Follow C11 round 2: priority order, verify never dropped, advice changed for both surfaces.

If the content text alone fits, only `structured_content` is dropped: `structured()` already put the same JSON in the content, so nothing is lost and no marker is needed. Until their own items land, `run`, `check`, `claim` and `prose` are held under the bound by the backstop alone.
why: Follow C8 round 2: two-step reduction, verify preserved.

text: **`query`.** Listings page, with two parameters that each mean one thing. `from` is always an id: the record a listing starts at, or the dependent `deps` starts at. A trailer names the next `from`. Labels and text in a listing are cut to `ENTRY_CAP`. A fact whose extents alone would overflow a page gets a page to itself, with its surplus extents counted, and the count names the call that reads them: `id` with `extent_from`. Asked for by `id`, a fact comes back with its labels uncut and its extents paged by `extent_from`, and a claim, which has no extents, comes back whole. A single label longer than the budget is cut, and says so. The CLI gets the same flags, so the two surfaces do not diverge.
